entries.content_osis: Num 21:1-3 <div eID="gen1869" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen1870" type="x-p"/> Victory of Israel over the Canaanitish King of Arad. - When this Canaanitish king, who dwelt in the Negeb, i.e., the south of Palestine (vid., Num 13:17), heard that Israel was coming the way of the spies, he made war upon the Israelites, and took some of them prisoners. <hi type="italic">Arad</hi> is mentioned both here and in the parallel passage, Num 33:40, and also by the side of <hi type="italic">Hormah</hi>, in <reference osisRef="Josh.12.14">Jos 12:14</reference>, as the seat of a Canaanitish king (cf. Jdg 1:16-17). According to <hi type="italic">Eusebius</hi> and <hi type="italic">Jerome</hi> in the <hi type="italic">Onomast</hi>., it was twenty Roman miles to the south of Hebron, and has been preserved in the ruins of <hi type="italic">Tell Arad</hi>, which v. Schubert (ii. pp. 457ff.) and Robinson (ii. pp. 473, 620, and 624) saw in the distance; and, according to <hi type="italic">Roth</hi> in <hi type="italic">Petermann's</hi> geographische Mittheilungen (1858, p. 269), it was situated to the south-east of Kurmul (Carmel), in an undulating plain, without trees or shrubs, with isolated hills and ranges of hills in all directions, among which was <hi type="italic">Tell Arad</hi>. The meaning of האתרים שדרך is uncertain. The lxx, <hi type="italic">Saad</hi>., and others, take the word <hi type="italic">Atharim</hi> as the proper name of a place not mentioned again; but the <hi type="italic">Chaldee</hi>, <hi type="italic">Samar</hi>., and <hi type="italic">Syr</hi>. render it with much greater probability as an appellative noun formed from תּוּר with א <hi type="italic">prosthet</hi>., and synonymous with התּרים, the spies (Num 14:6). The way of the spies was the way through the desert of Zin, which the Israelitish spies had previously taken to Canaan (Num 13:21). The territory of the king of Arad extended to the southern frontier of Canaan, to the desert of Zin, through which the Israelites went from Kadesh to Mount Hor. The Canaanites attacked them when upon their march, and made some of them prisoners.

As the Edomites refused a passage through their land when the Israelites left Mount Hor, they were obliged to take the way to the Red Sea, in order to go round the land of Edom, that is to say, to go down the Arabah to the head of the Elanitic Gulf.

entries.content_osis: Num 21:10-20 <div eID="gen1878" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen1879" type="x-p"/> March of Israel round Edom and Moab, to the Heights of Pisgah in the Field of Moab (cf. Num 33:41-47). - Num 21:10. From the camp in the Arabah, which is not more particularly described, where the murmuring people were punished by fiery serpents, Israel removed to <hi type="italic">Oboth</hi>. According to the list of stations in Num 33:41., they went from Hor to <hi type="italic">Zalmonah</hi>, the situation of which has not been determined; for <hi type="italic">C. v. Raumer's</hi> conjecture (<hi type="italic">der Zug der Israeliten, </hi>p. 45), that it was the same place as the modern <hi type="italic">Maan</hi>, has no firm basis in the fact that Maan is a station of the Syrian pilgrim caravans. From <hi type="italic">Zalmonah</hi> they went to <hi type="italic">Phunon</hi>, and only then to <hi type="italic">Oboth</hi>. The name <hi type="italic">Phunon</hi> is no doubt the same as <hi type="italic">Phinon</hi>, a tribe-seat of the Edomitish Phylarch (<reference osisRef="Gen.36.41">Gen 36:41</reference>); and according to <hi type="italic">Jerome</hi> (<hi type="italic">Onom. s. v. Fenon</hi>), it was “a little village in the desert, where copper was dug up by condemned criminals (see at <reference osisRef="Gen.36.41">Gen 36:41</reference>), between Petra and Zoar.” This statement suits very well, provided we imagine the situation of Phunon to have been not in a straight line between Petra and Zoar, but more to the east, between the mountains on the edge of the desert. For the Israelites unquestionably went from the southern end of the Arabah to the eastern side of Idumaea, through the Wady <hi type="italic">el Ithm</hi> (<hi type="italic">Getum</hi>), which opens into the Arabah from the east, a few hours to the north of Akaba and the ancient Ezion-geber. They had then gone round the mountains of Edom, and begun to “turn to the north” (<reference osisRef="Deut.2.3">Deu 2:3</reference>), so that they now proceeded farther northwards, on the eastern side of the mountains of Edom, “through the territory of the sons of Esau,” no doubt by the same road which is taken in the present day by the caravans which go from Gaza to Maan, through the Ghor. “This runs upon a grassy ridge, forming the western border of the coast of Arabia, and the eastern border of the cultivated land, which stretches from the land of Edom to the sources of the Jordan, on the eastern side of the Ghor” (v. <hi type="italic">Raumer</hi>, Zug, p. 45). On the western side of their mountains the Edomites had refused permission to the Israelites to pass through their land (Num 20:18.), as the mountains of Seir terminate towards the Ghor (the Arabah) in steep and lofty precipices, and there are only two or three narrow wadys which intersect them from west to east; and of these the Wady Ghuweir is the only one which is practicable for an army, and even this could be held so securely by a moderate army, that no enemy could force its way into the heart of the country (see <hi type="italic">Leake</hi> in <hi type="italic">Burckhardt</hi>, pp. 21, 22; and Robinson, ii. p. 583). It was different on the eastern side, where the mountains slope off into a wide extent of table-land, which is only slightly elevated above the desert of Arabia. Here, on the weaker side of their frontier, the Edomites lost the heart to make any attack upon the Israelites, who would now have been able to requite their hostilities. But the Lord had commanded Israel not to make war upon the sons of Esau; but when passing through their territory, to purchase food and water from them for money (<reference osisRef="Deut.2.4-Deut.2.6">Deu 2:4-6</reference>). The Edomites submitted to the necessity, and endeavoured to take advantage of it, by selling provisions, “in the same way in which, at the present day, the caravan from Mecca is supplied with provisions by the inhabitants of the mountains along the pilgrim road” (<hi type="italic">Leake</hi> in <hi type="italic">Burckhardt</hi>, p. 24). The situation of Oboth cannot be determined.

Num 21:22 and Num 20:17); and Sihon refused this request, just as the king of Edom had done, and marched with all his people against the Israelites. Sihon came out against the Israelites into the desert as far as <hi type="italic">Jahza</hi>, where a battle was fought, in which he was defeated. The accounts of the <hi type="italic">Onom</hi>. concerning Jahza, which was situated, according to <hi type="italic">Eusebius</hi>, between <hi type="italic">Medamon</hi> (<hi type="italic">Medaba</hi>) and <hi type="italic">Debous</hi> (<hi type="italic">Dibon</hi>, see above), and according to Jerome, between <hi type="italic">Medaba</hi> and <hi type="italic">Deblatai</hi>, may be reconciled with the statement that it was in the desert, provided we assume that it was not in a straight line between the places named, but in a more easterly direction on the edge of the desert, near to the commencement of the Wady <hi type="italic">Wale</hi>, a conclusion to which the juxtaposition of <hi type="italic">Jahza</hi> and <hi type="italic">Mephaot</hi> in <reference osisRef="Josh.13.18">Jos 13:18</reference>; <reference osisRef="Josh.21.37">Jos 21:37</reference>, and <reference osisRef="Jer.48.21">Jer 48:21</reference>, also points (see at <reference osisRef="Josh.13.18">Jos 13:18</reference>).

entries.content_osis: Num 21:24-26 <div eID="gen1890" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen1891" type="x-p"/> Israel smote him with the edge of the sword, i.e., without quarter (see <reference osisRef="Gen.34.26">Gen 34:26</reference>), and took possession of his land “<hi type="italic">from Arnon (Mojeb) to the Jabbok, unto the children of Ammon,”</hi> i.e., to the upper Jabbok, the modern <hi type="italic">Nahr or Moiet Ammân</hi>. The <hi type="italic">Jabbok</hi>, now called <hi type="italic">Zerka</hi>, i.e., the blue, does not take its rise, as <hi type="italic">Seetzen</hi> supposed, on the pilgrim-road by the castle of <hi type="italic">Zerka</hi>; but its source, according to <hi type="italic">Abulfeda</hi> <hi type="italic">(tab. Syr.</hi> p. 91) and <hi type="italic">Buckingham</hi>, is the <hi type="italic">Nahr</hi> <hi type="italic">Ammân</hi>, which flowed down from the ancient capital of the Ammonites, and was called the <hi type="italic">upper Jabbok</hi>, and formed the western border of the Ammonites towards the kingdom of Sihon, and subsequently towards Gad (<reference osisRef="Deut.2.37">Deu 2:37</reference>; <reference osisRef="Deut.3.16">Deu 3:16</reference>; <reference osisRef="Josh.12.2">Jos 12:2</reference>). “<hi type="italic">For the border of the Ammonites was strong”</hi> (firm), i.e., strongly fortified; “for which reason Sihon had only been able to push his conquests to the upper Jabbok, not into the territory of the Ammonites.” This explanation of <hi type="italic">Knobel's</hi> is perfectly correct; since the reason why the Israelites did not press forward into the country of the Ammonites, was not the strength of their frontier, but the word of the Lord, “Make not war upon them, for I shall give thee no possession of the land of the children of Ammon” (<reference osisRef="Deut.2.19">Deu 2:19</reference>). God had only promised the patriarchs, on behalf of their posterity, that He would give them the land of Canaan, which was bounded towards the east by the Jordan (Num 34:2-12; compared with <reference osisRef="Gen.10.19">Gen 10:19</reference> and <reference osisRef="Gen.15.19-Gen.15.21">Gen 15:19-21</reference>); and the Israelites would have received no settlement at all on the eastern side of the Jordan, had not the Canaanitish branch of the Amorites extended itself to that side in the time of Moses, and conquered a large portion of the possessions of the Moabites, and also (according to <reference osisRef="Josh.13.25">Jos 13:25</reference>, as compared with Jdg 11:13) of the Ammonites, driving back the Moabites as far as the Arnon, and the Ammonites behind the <hi type="italic">Nahr Ammân</hi>. With the defeat of the Amorites, all the land that they had conquered passed into the possession of the Israelites, who took possession of these towns (cf. <reference osisRef="Deut.2.34-Deut.2.36">Deu 2:34-36</reference>). The statement in Num 21:25, that Israel settled in all the towns of the Amorites, is somewhat anticipatory of the history itself, as the settlement did not occur till Moses gave the conquered land to the tribes of Reuben and Gad for a possession (Num 32). The only places mentioned here are <hi type="italic">Heshbon</hi> and her daughters, i.e., the smaller towns belonging to it (cf. <reference osisRef="Josh.13.17">Jos 13:17</reference>), which are enumerated singly in Num 32:34-38, and <reference osisRef="Josh.13.15">Jos 13:15</reference>-28. In explanation of the expression, “Heshbon and her daughters,” it is added in Num 21:26, that Heshbon was the city, i.e., the capital of the Amorite king Sihon, who had made war upon the former king of Moab, and taken away all his land as far as the Arnon. Consequently, even down to the time of the predecessor of Balak, the king of the Moabites at that time, the land to the north of the Arnon, and probably even as far as the lower Jabbok, to which point the kingdom of Sihon extended (see <reference osisRef="Deut.3.12-Deut.3.13">Deu 3:12-13</reference>; <reference osisRef="Josh.12.5">Jos 12:5</reference>), belonged to the Moabites. And in accordance with this, the country where the Israelites encamped opposite to Jericho, before crossing the Jordan, is reckoned as part of the land of Moab (<reference osisRef="Deut.1.5">Deu 1:5</reference>; <reference osisRef="Deut.29.1">Deu 29:1</reference>; <reference osisRef="Deut.32.49">Deu 32:49</reference>; <reference osisRef="Deut.34.5-Deut.34.6">Deu 34:5-6</reference>), and called Arboth Moab (see Num 22:1); whilst the women who seduced the Israelites to join in the idolatrous worship of Baal Peor are called daughters of Moab (Num 25:1).
